title: Serous Fluid Traps: Pericardial Cutoffs, Low Pleural Glucose, Secondary Peritonitis and Postpericardiotomy Syndrome
summary: Learn why pleural rules do not transfer to pericardial fluid, what else lowers pleural glucose, how to spot secondary peritonitis in ascites, and how postpericardiotomy syndrome is diagnosed.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 30 Hit 15 (postpericardiotomy syndrome), Exam Traps 2 (pericardial protein), 3 (low pleural glucose), 6 (Gram stain in ascites) and 7 (transudate vs exudate), and Table 2 (transudate/exudate comparison). Checked against Milevoj Kopcinovic & Culej 2014, Ege 2006, Malik 2021, Gabaldo 2019, Sinha 2016, Karkhanis & Joshi 2012, Rodríguez-Zarco 2019, Park & Choi 2020, the KASL 2018 ascites guideline, the BSG 2021 ascites guideline (Aithal) and Lu 2017. Trap 2 says to use Light’s criteria as the validated pericardial discriminator; the sources report Light’s specificity of only 72% in pericardial fluid, an unsatisfactory discriminatory accuracy in a later study, and exudate-range values in all pericardial fluids from bypass patients without pericardial disease (register flag rv-pericardial-light-criteria). Table 2/Trap 7 omit diuretic misclassification of heart-failure effusions (register flag rv-lights-diuretic-misclassification). Hit 15’s pericardial pH 7.35–7.45 with normal glucose was not found in any source read (register flag rv-pps-fluid-ph-glucose). Trap 6’s Gram stain sensitivity (~25%) and “>92% monomicrobial” figures were not found; a case report describes monomicrobial secondary peritonitis (register flag rv-sbp-gram-stain-figures). Pericardial protein >3.0 g/dL “22% specific” is not taught (only the 97% sensitivity was found, in Ege 2006). Not taught: traumatic-tap correction, Number Vault values beyond those listed.

objectives: Explain why pleural transudate/exudate cutoffs, including Light’s criteria, misclassify pericardial fluid and diuretic-treated heart-failure effusions.
List causes of low pleural fluid glucose besides infection, and state the parapneumonic drainage trigger.
Recognise ascitic fluid findings that point to secondary rather than spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
Describe the timing, proposed mechanism and diagnostic approach of postpericardiotomy syndrome.

scenes.title: Three fluids, three borrowed rules
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three serous fluids reach the bench. (1) Pericardial fluid from a patient two weeks after coronary bypass surgery: protein 3.4 g/dL and a fluid/serum LD ratio above 0.6. (2) Pleural fluid from a patient with rheumatoid arthritis and no pneumonia: glucose 25 mg/dL, Gram stain and culture negative. (3) Ascites from a patient with cirrhosis: neutrophils 2,400/µL and a Gram stain showing several kinds of bacteria. Question token: “Which rule is being borrowed?”

cues.text: Three fluids reach the bench. Pericardial fluid two weeks after bypass surgery, with protein of three point four grams per decilitre.
Pleural fluid with very low glucose, from a patient with rheumatoid arthritis and no pneumonia. And ascites in cirrhosis, with several kinds of bacteria on the Gram stain.
Each result tempts a quick label. Which rule is being borrowed where it does not belong?

scenes.title: Transudate, exudate and the normal pericardial sac
scenes.altText: Schematic: two cards. Transudate: systemic, non-inflammatory causes such as heart failure and cirrhosis; responds to treatment of the underlying disease. Exudate: inflammation or malignancy raises capillary permeability; pneumonia, cancer, tuberculosis, pulmonary embolism. Light’s criteria: ONE or more of fluid/serum protein ≥0.5, fluid/serum LD ≥0.6, fluid LD ≥2/3 of the serum upper limit = exudate. Diuretic card: up to about 25% of heart-failure pleural effusions are misclassified as exudates on diuretics; a serum–effusion albumin gradient above 12 g/L (1.2 g/dL) favours a transudate. Pericardium card: normal volume about 15–50 mL; small molecules similar to serum; LD about 2.5 times serum; protein about 0.6 of serum.

cues.text: A transudate comes from systemic, non-inflammatory problems such as heart failure or cirrhosis. An exudate comes from inflammation or tumour that makes capillaries leaky.
In pleural fluid, Light’s criteria call an exudate when any one ratio or level is high. But diuretics concentrate a heart-failure effusion, and up to a quarter are misclassified as exudates.
In that case an albumin gradient between serum and fluid of more than twelve grams per litre points back to a transudate.

The pericardial sac holds only about fifteen to fifty millilitres. In one study of normal pericardial fluid, LD was about two and a half times the serum level, and protein about sixty percent of serum.

scenes.title: Pericardial fluid and postpericardiotomy syndrome
scenes.altText: Pericardium card: biochemical data on pericardial fluid are scarce. In a prospective study, Light’s criteria identified pericardial exudates with sensitivity 98% and specificity 72%; a later study found the pericardial LD ratio, LD and protein ratio unsatisfactory discriminators. In 96 bypass patients (no pericardial disease), every pericardial fluid met Light’s exudate criteria. Postpericardiotomy card: new or worsening pericardial and/or pleural effusion, mostly 1–6 weeks after cardiac surgery (median 14 days in one series, 22 days in a registry); thought to be autoimmune (anti-heart antibodies); diagnosis needs at least two of five findings (fever without other cause, pleuritic/pericarditic chest pain, rub, pericardial effusion, pleural effusion with raised CRP); infection, malignancy, connective tissue disease and uraemia are ruled out first.

cues.text: Pericardial fluid has far less evidence behind it than pleural fluid. Light’s criteria pick up nearly every pericardial exudate, but in one prospective study their specificity was only seventy-two percent.
In ninety-six bypass patients without pericardial disease, every pericardial fluid met Light’s exudate criteria. So a pericardial protein or LD in the exudate range is not proof of an exudate.
Postpericardiotomy syndrome is a new or growing pericardial or pleural effusion, mostly one to six weeks after heart surgery. It is thought to be autoimmune, with antibodies against heart tissue.

It needs at least two of five findings, such as fever without another cause, chest pain, a rub, or new effusions with a raised CRP. Infection, cancer, connective tissue disease and uraemia must be ruled out first.

props.label: Diagnosis of exclusion: rule out the dangerous causes first

scenes.title: Low pleural glucose and mixed bacteria in ascites
scenes.altText: Glucose card: normal pleural glucose equals blood glucose; low = pleural/serum ratio below 0.5, seen with empyema, rheumatoid disease, lupus, tuberculosis, malignancy and oesophageal rupture; rheumatoid effusions characteristically have low glucose and pH. Drainage card: in parapneumonic effusion, pH below 7.20 indicates drainage; when pH is unavailable, glucose below 3.4 mmol/L (about 60 mg/dL) suggests a complicated effusion; in one analysis pH <7.2 had sensitivity 41%/specificity 94% and glucose <60 mg/dL 39%/97%. Ascites card: about 5% of cirrhotic patients with peritonitis have secondary bacterial peritonitis (perforation or abscess). Suspect it with neutrophils >1,000/µL, multiple organisms on Gram stain or culture, total protein ≥1 g/dL, LD above the serum upper limit, glucose ≤50 mg/dL, or no neutrophil fall after 48 h; ascitic CEA >5 ng/mL or ALP >240 U/L suggests perforation. Next: CT imaging and surgical evaluation.

cues.text: Normally pleural glucose matches blood glucose. A pleural-to-serum ratio below one half is low, and it is seen in empyema, rheumatoid disease, lupus, tuberculosis, cancer and oesophageal rupture.

For a parapneumonic effusion, a pH below seven point two zero points to drainage. Glucose below about sixty milligrams per decilitre is the fallback when pH is not available. Both are specific but miss many cases.
In ascites, a few patients with cirrhosis have secondary peritonitis from a perforation or abscess. Several organisms on Gram stain or culture are a warning sign.

So are very high neutrophils, protein of at least one gram, LD above the serum limit and glucose of fifty or less. High CEA or alkaline phosphatase suggests perforation, so get imaging and a surgical opinion.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Pericardial protein above 3 g/dL proves an exudate” (✓ normal pericardial fluid can reach exudate-range protein and LD; even Light’s criteria over-call exudates there); “Low pleural glucose means infection, so drain it” (✓ rheumatoid disease, lupus, tuberculosis and cancer lower glucose too; the parapneumonic drainage trigger is pH below 7.20 in the right setting); “Bacteria on an ascitic Gram stain mean SBP” (✓ several organisms suggest secondary peritonitis: image and call surgery).

cues.text: Trap one: pericardial protein above three grams proves an exudate. No: normal pericardial fluid can reach that range, and even Light’s criteria over-call exudates there.
Trap two: low pleural glucose means infection, so place a tube. No: rheumatoid disease, lupus, tuberculosis and cancer lower glucose too.
Trap three: bacteria on the ascitic Gram stain mean spontaneous peritonitis. No: several kinds of bacteria suggest a hole in the gut.

Where it breaks: secondary peritonitis can grow a single organism, especially with an abscess; Light’s criteria still catch nearly all true pericardial exudates; and low glucose is one clue, not a rule.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Pericardial fluid can look exudative when normal · low pleural glucose has many causes”, “Mixed bacteria in ascites → secondary peritonitis · postpericardiotomy = weeks later, exclude first”.

cues.text: Each serous sac needs its own rules, because normal pericardial fluid can look exudative, low pleural glucose has many causes besides infection, mixed bacteria in ascites point to a surgical leak, and postpericardiotomy syndrome is diagnosed only after dangerous causes are excluded.

props.label: Pericardium can look exudative · low pleural glucose ≠ infection only
Mixed bugs in ascites → secondary · PPS = weeks later, exclude first

explanation.what: Plain language: fluid can build up around the lungs, the heart or the bowel. Labs sort it into “pressure” fluid (transudate) and “inflamed” fluid (exudate), but the sorting rules were built for fluid around the lungs and do not carry over neatly. Normal fluid around the heart can already look “inflamed” on paper; low sugar in lung fluid can come from arthritis, lupus, tuberculosis or cancer as well as infection; several kinds of bacteria in belly fluid suggest a hole in the gut that needs a surgeon; and fluid that builds up a few weeks after heart surgery is often an immune reaction, called only after other causes are ruled out. Scientific terms: transudate, exudate, Light’s criteria, serum–effusion albumin gradient, pericardial effusion, parapneumonic effusion, empyema, rheumatoid pleurisy, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), secondary bacterial peritonitis, Runyon criteria, postpericardiotomy syndrome (PPS), post-cardiac injury syndrome.
explanation.why: Normal pericardial fluid has an LD about 2.5 times serum and protein about 0.6 of serum, so it already sits near or in the exudate range. Diuretics shift water out of a heart-failure effusion and concentrate protein and LD. Pleural glucose falls when cells, bacteria or inflamed pleura consume or block it, which happens in several diseases. Spontaneous peritonitis arises without a surgical source, whereas a perforated or abscessed bowel spills several organisms, protein and LD into ascites and consumes glucose. PPS is thought to follow an autoimmune response to injured pericardium and pleura.
explanation.measure: Light’s: any one of fluid/serum protein ≥0.5, fluid/serum LD ≥0.6, fluid LD ≥2/3 of serum upper limit = exudate (pleural). Diuretic check: serum–effusion albumin gradient >12 g/L favours transudate. Pericardial: Light’s sensitivity 98%, specificity 72% (one prospective study). Pleural glucose low = fluid/serum ratio <0.5; parapneumonic drainage if pH <7.20; glucose <3.4 mmol/L (about 60 mg/dL) when pH unavailable. Secondary peritonitis clues: neutrophils >1,000/µL, multiple organisms on Gram stain or culture, total protein ≥1 g/dL, LD above serum upper limit, glucose ≤50 mg/dL, no neutrophil fall at 48 h; CEA >5 ng/mL or ALP >240 U/L suggest perforation. PPS: mostly 1–6 weeks after surgery; at least 2 of 5 findings.
explanation.differs: Transudate (systemic, pressure-driven) vs exudate (local inflammation or tumour); spontaneous (no surgical source, treated with antibiotics) vs secondary peritonitis (perforation or abscess, needs imaging and surgical review); PPS (weeks after surgery, immune, diagnosis of exclusion) vs early postoperative bleeding or infection.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: a pericardial result that “meets” a pleural cutoff, a low pleural glucose in a non-infected patient, a polymicrobial ascitic Gram stain, and a post-surgical effusion weeks after bypass. The right answer usually rejects the borrowed rule and asks for the full clinical and laboratory picture.

comparisons.title: Transudate vs exudate

right.label: Exudate
points: Meets at least one Light’s criterion

comparisons.distinguisher: Pressure problem vs leaky, inflamed lining — but check the albumin gradient if diuretics may have concentrated a transudate.

comparisons.title: Spontaneous vs secondary bacterial peritonitis

right.label: Secondary
points: Multiple organisms; protein ≥ 1 g/dL; LD high; glucose ≤ 50

comparisons.distinguisher: Is there a hole or abscess in the abdomen that antibiotics alone cannot fix?

mnemonic.text: Every sac keeps its own rulebook: the Pericardium fools Light, Glucose has many eaters, and Mixed bugs mean a hole.
mnemonic.explanation: Links each serous space to the rule that does not transfer from pleural fluid.
mnemonic.limitation: Secondary peritonitis can grow a single organism, especially with an abscess; Light’s criteria still detect nearly all true pericardial exudates (high sensitivity, low specificity); low glucose is a supporting clue rather than a diagnostic rule.

analogyLimitations: Pericardial performance figures come from small single studies; cut-offs vary by laboratory and method.
takeaway: Each serous sac needs its own rules, because normal pericardial fluid can look exudative, low pleural glucose has many causes besides infection, mixed bacteria in ascites point to a surgical leak, and postpericardiotomy syndrome is diagnosed only after dangerous causes are excluded.

questions.stem: Pericardial fluid from a patient two weeks after coronary bypass surgery has protein 3.4 g/dL and a fluid/serum LD ratio of 0.9. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: The values are not proof of an exudate, because normal pericardial fluid can fall in the exudate range; interpret them with the clinical picture
options.rationale: Correct. Normal pericardial fluid LD is about 2.5 times serum, and in one study every pericardial fluid from bypass patients without pericardial disease met Light’s exudate criteria.

options.text: It is definitely a bacterial exudate and needs surgical drainage
options.rationale: Incorrect. Protein and LD ratios cannot identify infection, and in pericardial fluid they over-call exudates.

options.text: It is definitely a transudate because the patient recently had surgery
options.rationale: Incorrect. Surgery does not make the fluid a transudate; post-surgical effusions can be inflammatory, as in postpericardiotomy syndrome.

options.text: Apply the ascites albumin gradient of 1.1 g/dL to decide
options.rationale: Incorrect. The 1.1 g/dL serum–ascites albumin gradient was built for ascites and portal hypertension, not pericardial fluid.

questions.stem: A patient with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis and no signs of pneumonia has a lymphocytic pleural exudate with glucose 25 mg/dL; Gram stain and culture are negative. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Low pleural glucose also occurs in rheumatoid pleurisy, lupus, tuberculosis and malignancy, so it does not by itself mean infection
options.rationale: Correct. A pleural/serum glucose ratio below 0.5 is seen in empyema, rheumatoid disease, lupus, tuberculosis, malignancy and oesophageal rupture; rheumatoid effusions characteristically have low glucose.

options.text: Low glucose proves empyema, so a chest tube is mandatory
options.rationale: Incorrect. Glucose is not specific to infection; the drainage trigger in a parapneumonic effusion is mainly a pH below 7.20 in the right clinical setting.

options.text: Low glucose means the effusion is a transudate
options.rationale: Incorrect. Low pleural glucose is a feature of certain exudates, not transudates; this fluid is already an exudate.

options.text: The glucose result is invalid because pleural glucose normally runs far below blood glucose
options.rationale: Incorrect. Normal pleural glucose is about equal to blood glucose, because glucose diffuses freely across the pleura.

questions.stem: Ascites from a patient with cirrhosis shows neutrophils 2,400/µL, several different organisms on Gram stain, total protein 2.1 g/dL, glucose 30 mg/dL and LD above the serum upper limit. What should be suspected and done?

options.text: Secondary bacterial peritonitis: arrange abdominal imaging such as CT and a surgical evaluation
options.rationale: Correct. Multiple organisms, protein ≥1 g/dL, glucose ≤50 mg/dL and LD above the serum limit suggest secondary peritonitis, which needs imaging and consideration of surgery.

options.text: Typical spontaneous bacterial peritonitis: antibiotics alone, no further work-up
options.rationale: Incorrect. These findings fit secondary peritonitis, which antibiotics alone may not fix.

options.text: Contamination of the sample: repeat the paracentesis and ignore the result
options.rationale: Incorrect. A very high neutrophil count with low glucose and high LD is a real inflammatory picture, not simple contamination.
Incorrect. That term describes neutrophils ≥250/µL with a negative culture; here organisms are already seen, and several of them.

claims.text: Transudate vs exudate mechanisms and causes; Light’s criteria (any one); diuretics misclassify up to 25% of heart-failure effusions; albumin gradient >12 g/L favours transudate.

Pericardial data scarce; Light’s sensitivity 98%/specificity 72%; normal pericardial LD ~2.5× and protein ~0.6× serum; LD/protein ratios unsatisfactory; all bypass-patient pericardial fluids met exudate criteria; normal volume ~15–50 mL.

PPS mostly 1–6 weeks after cardiac surgery (median 14 days in one series); autoimmune hypothesis with anti-heart antibodies; at least two of five findings; diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out infection, malignancy, connective tissue disease and uraemia.
Normal pleural glucose equals blood; low ratio <0.5 in empyema, rheumatoid disease, lupus, TB, malignancy and oesophageal rupture; rheumatoid effusions characteristically low glucose and pH.
Parapneumonic pH <7.20 indicates drainage; glucose <3.4 mmol/L (about 60 mg/dL) when pH unavailable; pH and glucose specific but insensitive (41%/94%, 39%/97%).

Secondary peritonitis about 5%; clues: PMN >1,000, multiple organisms on Gram stain/culture, protein ≥1 g/dL, LD > serum ULN, glucose ≤50 mg/dL, no PMN fall at 48 h, CEA >5 or ALP >240; CT and surgical evaluation; SBP PMN ≥250 with immediate antibiotics; secondary peritonitis can be monomicrobial.

Reviewer figures not found in the sources read: pericardial protein >3.0 g/dL “only 22% specific”; PPS pericardial fluid pH 7.35–7.45 with normal glucose; ascitic Gram stain ~25% sensitive in SBP; SBP >92% monomicrobial.
claims.note: Not taught as facts in this lesson.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 30 Exam Trap 2 tells learners to use Light’s criteria as “the validated discriminator” for pericardial fluid. Milevoj Kopcinovic & Culej 2014 report Light’s specificity of only 72% for pericardial exudates, normal pericardial fluid LD about 2.5 times serum and protein about 0.6 of serum, and unsatisfactory discriminatory accuracy of the LD and protein ratios; Ege 2006 found that all pericardial fluids from 96 bypass patients met Light’s exudate criteria. The lesson teaches that pericardial results in the exudate range are not proof of an exudate (register flag rv-pericardial-light-criteria).

Ch. 30 Table 2 and Exam Trap 7 present “fails all Light’s criteria” as the pleural transudate rule without noting that diuretics concentrate heart-failure effusions. Milevoj Kopcinovic & Culej 2014 state up to 25% of cardiac pleural effusions are misclassified as exudates on diuretics and that a serum–effusion albumin gradient >12 g/L reclassifies them as transudates; the lesson teaches this (register flag rv-lights-diuretic-misclassification).

Ch. 30 Hit 15 states that postpericardiotomy syndrome fluid typically has pH within 7.35–7.45 and normal glucose. None of the sources read (Malik 2021, Gabaldo 2019, Sinha 2016, Milevoj Kopcinovic & Culej 2014) gives a typical pH or glucose for PPS fluid; they define PPS clinically (timing, at least two of five findings, exclusion of other causes). The lesson does not teach the pH/glucose claim (register flag rv-pps-fluid-ph-glucose).

Ch. 30 Exam Trap 6 gives an ascitic Gram stain sensitivity of ~25% in SBP and states that true SBP is >92% monomicrobial; neither figure was found in the sources read. The KASL 2018 and BSG 2021 guidelines support multiple organisms on Gram stain or culture as a clue to secondary peritonitis, and Lu 2017 describes a monomicrobial secondary peritonitis, so a single organism does not exclude a surgical source (register flag rv-sbp-gram-stain-figures).
